purpose: This medication is a combination birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It may also be prescribed to help regulate menstrual periods or reduce menstrual cramps. In some cases, doctors use it to treat acne or manage hormone-related symptoms.
how_it_works: This pill contains two hormones — a progestin called norgestrel and an estrogen called ethinyl estradiol — that work together to prevent pregnancy in three ways. First, they stop your ovaries from releasing an egg each month. Second, they thicken the mucus in your cervix so sperm have a harder time getting through. Third, they thin the lining of your uterus so that if an egg were somehow fertilized, it would have difficulty attaching.
common_side_effects: Nausea, especially when you first start taking it. Breast tenderness or swelling. Headaches. Spotting or light bleeding between periods. Mood changes. Decreased sex drive. Contact lens discomfort due to fluid changes in the eyes.
warnings: Do not smoke while taking this pill, especially if you are over 35, as it significantly raises the risk of serious blood clots, stroke, or heart attack. Tell your doctor if you have a history of blood clots, high blood pressure, migraines with aura, liver disease, or certain cancers. This pill does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections. Stop taking it and call your doctor right away if you have chest pain, sudden severe headache, vision changes, or leg pain or swelling.
typical_dosing: You take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Most packs have 28 pills — 21 active hormone pills followed by 7 reminder pills. You start a new pack right after finishing the old one with no break. Taking it at the same time every day helps it work best and reduces side effects like nausea.
